newsitem.title: USA: Vote-counting underway in Teamster battle.
newsitem.headline: Vote-counting underway in Teamster battle.

text.p: The hard-fought contest for the presidency of the 1.4 million-member Teamsters Union went into the home stretch Tuesday as officials began the task of counting nearly a half-million ballots.

The first returns available late Tueaday from two tiny locals in San Francisco and Memphis, Tenn., gave challenger James Hoffa an early, albeit irrelevant, lead of 21 votes over the 10 votes cast for Teamsters Union President Ron Carey.

Barring an unexpected landslide, a winner is not expected to be declared until Friday as the staff of a court-appointed election officer plods through the nearly 500,000 paper ballots that were mailed in over the past month by members of 560 Teamster locals throughout the United States and Canada.

Both campaigns expect a close race, a rare point of agreement in this bruising battle where each candidate accuses the other of being tied to unsavory characters, inept and unfit for a job that has a larger constituency than any two members of the House of Representatives.
As the local-by-local returns dribble in throughout the week, each side will seek out trends and voting patterns that it will try to use to predict the outcome.
"We're just tring to see if we're getting the votes out of them that we expected," said Carey spokeswoman Renee Asher.
Hoffa spokesman Richard Leebove said the increase in voter turnout over the previous Teamster election five years ago bodes well for the challenger.

Hoffa, 55, son of Jimmy Hoffa, the infamous Teamster leader of the 1950s and 1960s who is presumed to have been murdered by the mob in 1975, is a Detroit labour lawyer who has worked for the past three years at a Teamster joint council that was once headed by his father.

Hoffa has made an issue out of Carey's five-year record in office, which he says has left its finances depleted and its membership divided and demoralised. He has made a boost in strike pay a centrepiece of his campaign.
Carey, 60, a former United Parcel Service driver and dissident leader of a New York local, won his office as the darkhorse candidate in a three-way race in 1991.

The self-styled reformer blames the union's woes on many factors, including his predecessors' lavish spending and inattention to membership-building. He claims to have ended years of deficit spending and declining membership, touts his anti-corruption record and calls his opponent inexperienced.

The current election is only the second in the 93-year history of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters that has been open to all rank-and-file members. Previous presidents of the union that for years was the symbol of labour corruption were elected by convention delegates.

But in 1989 the union that saw three of its last six presidents go to prison settled a federal anti-racketeering suit by agreeing to hold open elections run by the government. The settlement also installed a panel of overseers with broad investigatory authority for an indefinite period of time.

Democracy, however, did not come cheap for the Teamsters. The government is expected to spend about $21 million on this election, including the cost for its vote-counting facility at the National 4-H Council centre here. The union picked up the tab for the 1991 election.
The candidates and their running mates have spent about $5.3 million on their campaigns, with Hoffa outspending Carey by more than two-to-one.
In the last election, only about 425,000 votes were cast by the union's 1.4 million members, but more than 28,000 were not counted because of voter error or candidate challenges.
The election officer, Barbara Zack Quindel, intends to announce official running totals in the races each afternoon for the remainder of the week.
